item.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
item.description: In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump's pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation. Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy's decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats. In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA's current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn't say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is "quite lethal" or that children are given vaccine doses the "size of a soda bottle." Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong. Read full article Comments

item.title: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation
item.description: null Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect." In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. (Image credit: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler) In the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy . The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun . In 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018. The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity. Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart. "I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar said. In the new study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun . "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar said. Although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. item.title: Anthropic decides to go head-to-head with GTA VI release, schedules IPO for the same day
item.description: Well, it’s official: Anthropic will become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab in history come the opening of markets on Thursday. The company kicked off its IPO roadshow last week, announcing plans to offer 825 million shares with an IPO price between $70 and $78 a share when sales begin Thursday. The company's most recent SEC filing cites that price range but allows for the possibility of a higher price, which should be determined Wednesday night. Late on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Anthropic would price at $83, citing people familiar. Whatever the case, Anthropic is likely to be valued at more than $1 trillion. Anthropic’s debutante ball has been on the horizon for a while, and documents leaked in late September made it all the more inevitable as the company’s finances revved up and it sought to capture the momentum of its best quarter to date before things start to tail off. The company revised its IPO documents on November 2, warning that the 12x growth it was touting was unlikely to continue in the long term due to compute infrastructure investments to the tune of nearly $900 billion it was on the hook for over the next few years. "In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the revised prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all." It’s possible, in other words, that Anthropic may never be a money maker despite the hype and its position as the first mover. The IPO prospectus is short on answers to critical questions and leaves a lot unanswered - like, for example, whether it’s going to actually be able to pay its bills. "Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the updated prospectus admits. Investors don’t seem to care right now, though. Anthropic already has compute commitments amounting to roughly $70.7 billion in the next 12 months. That’s just shy of its $81 billion run-rate as of October 31. Expect more hot air to be injected tomorrow, adding additional surface tension and the possibility of even more losses if, and when, this monster pops. ®

item.title: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites
item.description: Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX. These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services. “At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register . “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.” As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years. Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently. Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.” “We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.” NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million ), and F5 maintains the open source version. On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible. CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 , both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5. “Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.” Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concep t to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8. item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water
item.description: null On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars. The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago. MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars . The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface , and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place. An Atlas V rocket launches NASA's Mars MAVEN orbiter into space from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Base on Nov. 18, 2013. (Image credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls) Why it mattered NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind , as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time. After its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014 . The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind. An artist's view of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft at Mars on a mission to study its upper atmosphere. (Image credit: NASA) "The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come." MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study. NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent , with NASA losing communication with the orbiter. An investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). item.title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
item.description: Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core . Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. " The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance. item.title: To rank the world's biggest supercomputers, we're gonna need a bigger bench
item.description: For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers. With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world. Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today. “These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week. It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with. And some believe it may be time for a rethink. “What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said. For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity. What happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he said. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.” By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster. “Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained. This is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier said. They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference. Because of this, Strohmaier says, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus. But these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system. What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a new benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler said. Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4. Another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters

item.title: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why
item.description: null More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished. Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past. Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth . Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years. But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged. In the Grand Canyon, rock layers separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, revealing a vast gap in Earth's geological record. (Image credit: Marcia Straub via Getty Images) One of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity. It's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years. "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana said in a statement . "The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance." The Great Unconformity imaged here shows 550 million year old Tapeats Sandstone resting on 1.7 billion year old Vishnu Schist, in Blacktail Canyon along the Colorado River in Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona. (Image credit: William Dummitt via Getty Images) What erased the geological record? In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame. Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years. The results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier. But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps

item.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
item.description: International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings. After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it " shameful " and a " national embarrassment ." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week. But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic. Read full article Comments

item.title: ULA traces Vulcan Centaur rocket failure to 'inadequate fuel supply' to 1st-stage engines
item.description: null United Launch Alliance (ULA) is getting a handle on why its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed over the weekend. That failure, which occurred during a launch from Florida's Space Coast on Sunday (Nov. 15), led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites . ULA soon traced the anomaly to Vulcan Centaur's first stage , and it has now pinpointed the problem area even further. "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an update today (Nov. 18). This is good news for Blue Origin , Jeff Bezos' aerospace company, which builds the BE-4. Two of these engines power Vulcan's first-stage booster, and they're also key to Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket: That heavy lifter features seven or nine BE-4s in its first stage, depending on the configuration. (New Glenn has its own issues at the moment; it exploded during a test on May 28 , and Blue Origin is working to return the powerful rocket to flight.) ULA had already said that Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters (SRBs) and its Centaur V upper stage — which employs a different engine, the RL-10 — seem to perform well on Sunday. Further analysis is firming up that conclusion, according to today's update. Vulcan has had issues with its SRBs in the past. On the rocket's second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds into flight. On both occasions, Vulcan overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payload to orbit. In the wake of the February flight, ULA and Northrop Grumman, which builds the SRBs, tweaked the nozzle design — a fix that apparently worked, based on Sunday's nominal performance. Vulcan Centaur rises into the sky on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: ULA) Sunday's launch was the fifth ever for the two-stage Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has now experienced issues on three of its five flights, though Sunday's was the only one that ended in failure. Vulcan was out of action for about nine months after the February SRB issue. It's unclear how long its current grounding will last; that depends on what ULA's anomaly investigation, which the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing, ends up finding.

They explored content ownership, audience engagement, monetisation and the importance of meaningful brand relationships. The discussions reflected an increasingly important question for the industry: How can creators turn the audiences and cultural influence they have built into sustainable businesses? item.title: Ibukun Awosika, Juliet Ibrahim, Bola Adesola & More: Leading Women Take Centre Stage at The Executive Woman Summit 2.0
item.description: What does it really mean to play to win in business and leadership? Beyond earning a seat at the table, it requires more than competence or professional accomplishments. It requires the confidence to own one’s value, the clarity to communicate one’s contributions and the intentionality to build visibility that translates into meaningful influence. These conversations defined The Executive Woman Summit (TEWS) 2.0 , which brought together hundreds of executive women, corporate professionals, entrepreneurs and emerging leaders at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Convened by Bola Matel-Okoh , a dual-qualified attorney (called to both the New York and Nigerian Bars), Executive Coach, Non-Executive Director at Wema Bank, and CEO of BMO Advisory Services , the second edition of the summit was themed Playing to Win: Elevate Your Vision, Value and Visibility. It provided an intentional platform for candid conversations, practical insights and strategic alliances on what it takes for women to advance, lead and thrive in today’s evolving corporate landscape. In her opening address, Matel-Okoh challenged women to rethink how they approach professional visibility, authority and advancement. According to her, competence is merely the baseline; it is not enough if you are unwilling to communicate your value, own your voice and position yourself for higher-stakes opportunities. This philosophy also came through in her cover interview with THISDAY Glitterati ahead of the summit, where she offered a compelling perspective on the distinction between holding a powerful position and exercising genuine influence. “A powerful position gives you formal authority. Influence determines how deeply your leadership shapes people’s thinking, decisions and actions. A title may secure your place in a meeting, but credibility makes people listen,” she explained. She also challenged the assumption that excellent work will automatically speak for itself, encouraging women to communicate their contributions with evidence and confidence. “What problem did you solve? What result did you produce? What changed because of your leadership?” she asked, highlighting the importance of making professional value visible to the decision-makers who influence career progression and boardroom opportunities. “There is no need to diminish your achievements to make others comfortable. You can be gracious and still be clear about the value you bring,” she added. The summit featured a distinguished line-up of women shaping leadership, business, finance, entertainment and corporate governance. Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria, Bola Adesola , and CEO of FS Global Advisory Services, Folake Sanu , delivered keynote addresses, sharing perspectives on leadership, professional growth, boardroom dynamics and navigating the demands of executive life. Bringing together industry leaders, policymakers, corporate executives and other distinguished guests, the evening marked six years of WIEN’s advocacy for greater representation, inclusion and leadership opportunities for women across the energy value chain. Beyond the glamour, elegant conversations and celebrations, the event carried a clear message: it is time to move beyond conversations about inclusion and focus on measurable progress. item.title: California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps
item.description: Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles. California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide. The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel. Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety." On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco. The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online , a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic. "The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement. Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18. Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco. A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater . A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US. "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. "We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog , driving into telephone poles , and killing cats and dogs . ®

item.title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
item.description: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference , but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning . According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services. To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware. It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too. In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site. “That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware. The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime , an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is

item.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
item.description: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analy

item.title: 'A shotgun marriage': Why are NASA's SkyFall Mars helicopters riding on a nuclear rocket?
item.description: null The pace is picking up on building, testing, and plotting out the flight paths for a trio of NASA Ingenuity-class helicopters to investigate Mars after riding there on a nuclear-powered rocket. NASA's Skyfall mission will see those mini-choppers dropped off at Mars by the space agency's Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1) rocket, the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft slated for launch in late 2028. After its cruise phase and initial Mars flyby in 2029, that nuclear carrier craft will make a second Mars approach in the Fall of 2030 to unleash a SkyFall entry capsule outfitted with a fleet of small aerial vehicles that will soar across the Red Planet . But some experts are questioning why NASA is combining two such high-profile missions into one. "It is clear that SkyFall was approved for programmatic or political reasons," said Scott Hubbard, former director of NASA's Ames Research Center and the first Mars Program Director (aka the " Mars Czar ") at NASA Headquarters, told Space.com. "The connection to Space Reactor-1 seems to me to be a bit of a shotgun marriage, a tech-demo piggybacking on another mission as an opening bid for a 'nuclear NASA.'" Shotgun marriage? Hubbard is a retired adjunct professor of aeronautics and astronautics at Stanford University. He is a major voice in shaping Red Planet exploration goals, drawing upon his expertise as NASA's former foremost Mars authority. His understanding is that the basic concept had been developed as a follow on to Ingenuity, an attempt to move beyond a technology demo and into a science platform. Hubbard said that combining these two observations, the outcome presents "an unusual set of management issues." Since the SkyFall mission concept first appeared, he said, the usual sequence for a science mission is reversed. "The science community is having to scramble to back into a set of requirements and objectives that match the SkyFall capabilities. Fortunately the community is very creative," said Hubbard, "and the basic Planetary Decadal objectives are very broad." Decadal surveys reflect a broad consensus within the scientific community and provide detailed insights into the strategic priorities and mission directives set for the next decade across key scientific domains, including planetary exploration. Lemonade squeeze However, Hubbard said he has heard griping about the "fait accompli" process, "but the planetary community will make lemonade." It should be noted however, Hubbard continued, that this process is not how you would design a strategic set of missions as precursors for human exploration. "SR-1 Freedom is a technology demo that may or may not be ready for the Mars launch window in 2028. It is clear that the Mars Program has a standard launch concept in their back pocket," said Hubbard. "Nuclear Electric Propulsion [NEP] is of little value in traveling to Mars, not shaving any time off the transit. The real value of NEP is for risk reduction, use at the moon, ou

item.title: 'Project Hail Mary' is heading back to theaters this December
item.description: null Fist my bump, everyone, because box office smash hit "Project Hail Mary" is heading back to theaters this December. The exceptional sci-fi movie, based on Andy Weir's book, stars Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who becomes key to saving the world. Together with Rocky, an alien he meets along the way, Grace must solve the riddle of the mysterious substance that's causing the sun (and Rocky's star) to die out. Amazon MGM has revealed the return to theaters with a video showcasing the many accolades that the film received. "Project Hail Mary" returns to the big screen on Dec. 11 and will be shown in all formats, including IMAX and 70MM. Ryan Gosling upside down floating in zero gravity in Project Hail Mary (2026). (Image credit: MGM) "Project Hail Mary" was a massive success for Amazon MGM, grossing over $600 million worldwide when it first dropped in theaters back in March 2026. It was also a huge hit with critics, scoring an average of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes , and more importantly, getting two big thumbs up in our review ! Dec. 11 is a smart choice by MGM too, as it puts the sci-fi spectacle back in front of audiences a week ahead of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. That's not a battle you want to get in the middle of. If you missed "Project Hail Mary" in theaters the first time, I'd definitely recommend you try to catch one of these screenings. It's a beautiful movie — visually and emotionally — and it deserves to be seen on the big screen. If you're not feeling up to a trip to the theaters, you can also catch "Project Hail Mary" from the comfort of your own home, as it's also streaming on Amazon Prime Video. item.title: The wrong setting for AI cache can cost you a lot of cash
item.description: Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice. Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning. Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze. Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background. The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again. "After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads." There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made. They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy. "I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation." The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond. It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app. "I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits." Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong , just with customer requests. The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud , and it appears the lessons need to be learned again. Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we'r

item.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
item.description: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the

item.title: PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road
item.description: Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement. It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, " be removed from a future version of Windows ," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default. After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties. PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless. PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover , who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude. PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain. The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time. Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts. Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft. Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself. "Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead. Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®

item.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
item.description: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

item.title: Supernova explodes before astronomers' eyes | Space photo of the day for Nov. 18, 2026
item.description: null Before-and-after photos showing the appearance of a new supernova designated SN 2026ahvu. (Image credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)) A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth. What is it? Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf . During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion. Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter. This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place. Why is it incredible? Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres. ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system. But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova. Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

item.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
item.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

item.title: StubHub International warns customer data may have left the venue
item.description: Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals. The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November. Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings. StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact. The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity. Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing. "To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords , banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently. "However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations." The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond. Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns. In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices. StubHub International also recently faced criticism for allowing a single ticket tout to advertise £1 million worth of U2 tickets, despite its stated opposition to ticket-buying bots. ®

item.title: The Lego Star Trek bridge diorama set should be your gateway to finally watching the Original Series
item.description: null It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek . Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it. But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch. And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets. Boldly building where no one has built before Building the Lego Star Trek: Bridge diorama. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently. Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built. As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty. There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk. The minifigure bridge crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise (L-R): Nurse Chapel, Chekov, Scotty, Spock, Kirk, McCoy, Uhura and Sulu. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge: $199.99 Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series". View Deal Alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though. It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with c

item.title: Business as usual, but Huang ain't coming back, says Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago. The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute. Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year. Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. item.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
item.description: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaul

item.title: India's SatLeo Labs wants to build a 'thermometer for Earth' in space
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time. SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a " thermometer for Earth " in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence , the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says. "It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview. That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs. The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches . Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai. "We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth ," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO. First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology. Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. item.title: Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
item.description: Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses. City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available. Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025. Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses. City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization. Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket. "Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police. "Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating. "This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice." The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud. Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people. Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category. "The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales.
